metabolic syndrome, as defined by the International Diabetes Federation, is a strong risk factor for the development of hypertension and cardiovascular disease, independent of other risk factors, such as smoking, obesity and dyslipidaemia.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pulse pressure is higher and heart rate is faster in patients with hypertension who have metabolic syndrome than those without.
the metabolic syndrome is associated to a worse cardiometabolic profile, which includes increased pulse pressure and heart rates, in hypertensive patients.
the metabolic syndrome increases cardiovascular risk, in part, through increased arterial stiffness, which in turn increases pulse pressure and heart-rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic syndrome may be associated with increased arterial stiffness and/or increased sympathetic tone in hypertensive out-patients.

metabolic syndrome is associated not only with an increased risk of diabetes, but also with an increased pulse pressure and heart rhythm, which are both associated with an increased cardiovascular risk.

metabolic syndrome is associated, independently of other factors, with higher pulse pressure and heart rates in patients with hypertension, which might contribute to the increased cardiovascular risk associated with metabolic syndrome.
